What is the Tonj First? 
Tonj First Movement is non-political and non-tribal Movement formed by some individuals of Tonj to fight for government's neglect,violation of human rights,under development and Tonj insecurity[undergoing communal violence]. This Movement represents all voices of Tonj South, North and East both at home and in diaspora who say 'ENOUGH IS ENOUGH'. We are non-violence group advocating for rights and justice of our abandoned people.
"TONJ FIRST MOVEMENT". A chronicle of citizens Reslove.
Phase 1:
Tonj citizens have been watching the useless communal violence back home for decades and chosen to be quite..thinking government will intervene and solve the problems among the disputing communities  but failed to solve and provide mutual security to the people of Tonj. Tonj is a community known for its quiet rhythms and close-knit geographical area, witnessed a turning point when its people rose to demand for change. The Tonj First Movement emerged not from a single voice, but from a growing chorus of voices, desperate citizens who had seen too many reckless deaths and massive destruction back home and felt the cruel weight of political repression as capable leaders were imprisoned without justification for almost 2 years as well. Tonj First Movement is a Movement born of grief,courage and a fierce belief that ordinary people of Tonj deserve a say in the fate of their own rights. 
The root causes of the Movement lay in a chain of grievances that could not be ignored. Reckless deaths, whether from violence, neglect or inadequate protection, eroded trust in the institutions meant to safeguard the lives and exercise the rule of law. The imprisonment of Tonj capable leaders, people who had attempted to channel the community's pain into constructive action has also created a vacuum of leadership and a sense of powerlessness. In thier absence, their families as well as Tonj community were left to navigate fear and uncertainty and the once-stable social fabric began to fray. Tonj First Movement crystallised as a collective demand of accountability, transparency and an environment in which peaceful co-existence, lawful expression could occur without fear of arbitrary detention or untimely consequences. 
What began as small, courageous acts, silent vigils, orderly marches and earnest conversations in communities and courtyards grew into a broader assertion of civic identity. The people of Tonj are assembled around shared grievances while insisting on non-violence and dignity. Tonj First Movement sought to elevate the concerns of ordinary residents to the levels of public policy, pressing for investigations into deaths, human rights and the release or fair trial of Tonj politicians detained for political reasons. The Movement emphasised that change could come through organised, lawful means: dialogue with authoritarians, educating local people and creation of safe spaces where grievances could be aired and addressed. 
To the government, the Tonj First Movement  demonstrated a disciplined commitment to peaceful protest and the rule of law, even when the government didn't always respond promptly or adequately. The participants are young and old, men and women, shared a common conviction, that Tonj lives deserved to be protected, leadership which is answerable. Tonj community should not have to endure the punishment of unresolved violence or arbitrary confinement. At this point, if Tonj community unresolved killings remain constant like this, Tonj community will not participate in the forthcoming elections. Elections are for people who are free from hunger, conflicts and human rights violation but not people whose sufferings are not given attention like Tonj community. Tonj remains as a warring zone where reckless activities are taking place, raiding, revenge killings and night attacks which involve women, elderly people and children. Tonj First Movement has condemned those activities against Tonj people. Tonj community needs schools, hospitals, security, roads, clean drinking water not elections, guns and ammunitions. SPLM should stop seeking votes from Tuonj instead of providing security. Enough is enough.. Young people of Tonj wake up..
In reflection, the Tonj First Movement represents more than a Movement of protest for rights, justice and freedom. It embodies the enduring spirit of citizens who refuse to surrender their rights in the face of fear.
Best regards,
Afri Wol Mathiang,
Law student at the University of Nairobi, 
Member of Tonj First Movement for rights and justice of Tonjians. See less

TONJ FIRST - OUR PEOPLE, OUR RESPONSIBILITY 
 Deng Clinton

TONJ FIRST
WHO WE ARE
TONJ FIRST is not a political party. It is not a tribe. It is a PEOPLE'S MOVEMENT born from the heart of Tonj - Greater Tonj, Tonj North, Tonj South, Tonj East.
We are the sons and daughters of Tonj, both at home and in diaspora, who say *ENOUGH IS ENOUGH.
OUR CALL
1. FREE OUR LEADERS
Our leaders are not criminals. They are our voice. We demand justice, not revenge. We demand due process, dialogue, and freedom. You cannot build peace by locking up the fathers of the community. Free them, hear them, bring them to the table.
2. OUR RESPONSIBILITY
Tonj is our mother. If we don't build it, no one will. Security, schools, hospitals, roads it is OUR responsibility, not UN, not Juba alone. We must stop waiting and start acting.
3. OUR PEOPLE
Before party, before payam, before clan we are Tonj people. Dinka, Jur, Balanda all Tonj. Your pain is my pain. Your child is my child. No Tonj child should die of hunger or gun again.
4. ONE LOVE
One Tonj, One Heart, One Love. We are tired of division. The politicians divided us to rule us. We say: We are brothers again. Lou, Lou paher,Apuk, Bongo, Jalwau, Nyang, Thony, Apuk juwiir, Luacjang,Yar, Luackoth, Thiik, Abuok, Atok & Noi we are ONE.
5. RESPECT THE DIGNITY OF OUR HEROES
Our heroes did not die for us to fight each other. From Anyanya to SPLA — they died for peace, for dignity. Respect them by stopping cattle raiding, revenge killing, and insulting our elders on social media.
6. STOP THE FIGHT & BE IN PEACE
The gun has never built a classroom. Enough blood. Enough revenge. Enough communal fighting.
Let the sons of Tonj put the guns down and pick up books, plows, and footballs. Peace is not weakness Peace is power.
OUR MOTTO
If Tonj is peaceful, South Sudan will be peaceful. If Tonj rises, South Sudan rises.
TONJ FIRST is:
- Youth for Peace
- Women for Peace
- Elders
Your Faithful Bro
Aldo Achuil Mangok

Free Tito Duang Dhieu: We Cannot Just Sit Back While People Suffer!
By: Bol Garang Agany
London, United Kingdom
23rd August 2026
Word went around last week from several sources, including Radio Tamazuj, that Chief Duang Dhieu Duang—better known as Tito Majok Hello—had been detained. The National Security Service reportedly detained the Paramount Chief of Gomjuer Centre and took him to Aweil town.
Why was he detained? Because he went to Nyamlel Central Prison and took photographs and videos showing the terrible conditions inside. He visited the prison after an inmate reportedly died from hunger and illness. Tito wanted to bring the situation to light so that ordinary people could step in and help those who were suffering.
This isn’t just another news story to me. Chief Tito is a great friend of mine.
Nearly ten years ago, when I left home and headed abroad, I met him along the way. We already knew each other, but that journey helped us bond on a deeper level. As a young man leaving my family behind for the first time, I was terrified of what lay ahead. But whenever Tito was around, it felt like having a big brother by my side. He gave me confidence at a time when everything else was uncertain.
I won’t go on about how kind he is here; anyone who knows him can vouch for that. Even when he was extremely busy in Khartoum, he always made time to check up on me. Whenever he visited the city, he would come and see how I was getting on with my studies at Comboni College.
I really cannot stress enough how much he looked out for me.
That’s why reading about his arrest made my blood boil.
From what has been reported, Tito didn’t go to Nyamlel Prison to cause trouble or stir things up. He went there, saw human beings living in absolute misery, and refused to simply walk away. He took photographs to expose the reality to the public.
This is where we need to ask a very simple question:
What did he actually do wrong by speaking up for our people?
Look at those photographs. Anyone with a bit of heart would find it difficult to look away.
These are human beings. They may be prisoners, but they have not lost their humanity. They still need food, clean water, medical care and basic dignity.
When someone is dying from starvation and illness inside a prison, we should be talking about how to save lives and fix the conditions—not turning on the person who pointed out the problem.
Tito saw a crisis and spoke up. In my view, he did the right thing.
Instead of coming down hard on him for taking photographs, the authorities should explain why prisoners are being forced to live in such conditions in the first place.
That is the real issue we must not dodge.
We cannot keep quiet while those in power try to silence citizens. When something is wrong, we have to call it out.
The old days are gone. We are living in a digital age where information can move from Nyamlel to the rest of the world within seconds. You cannot hide people who are suffering and expect the world not to know about it.
People today know their rights. They ask tough questions, pass information along and demand answers.
You cannot simply sweep this issue under the carpet.
When a citizen is taken away and his whereabouts are unknown, the public has every right to ask where he is, why he was taken, and what legal procedures are being followed.
This whole situation raises serious questions about basic rights and due process. We need answers.
No one is saying chiefs are above the law. Nobody 
is.
But the law is supposed to protect citizens too—especially those who stand up against injustice.
If there was a problem with how Tito handled the situation, then proper legal channels should be used to address it. Detention should not be used to intimidate people or scare others into silence.
Today it is Tito. Tomorrow it could be any of us.
That is exactly why we cannot stay silent.
Some people will not agree with me, and that’s fine. But sensible people can agree on one basic principle:
When people are suffering, you address the suffering; you do not silence the person who exposed it.
We have to stop shrugging things off simply because the person affected is not our brother, sister or relative. Our own rights are only secure when we are willing to stand up for each other.
Chief Tito, wherever you are being held, know that you are not alone.
I know you as a good and compassionate man. I will never forget how much you supported me when I was just a young man trying to find my way, and many others can say the same.
You saw people suffering, and you refused to look the other way.
You spoke up, and I stand with you firmly.
Free Tito Duang Dhieu!

The Village That Chose Peace 
Once upon a time, there was a beautiful village divided by hatred, mistrust, discrimination, and conflict. People stopped visiting one another, families became separated, and young people grew up believing that those from another community were their enemies. The village had everything it needed to prosper, fertile land, hardworking people, talented youth, and natural resources. But because of division, they could not develop together.  One day, a courageous young man stood before the community and asked:
“If we continue fighting one another, who will build our schools?  Who will protect our children? Who will develop our farms and businesses? And what kind of future are we leaving for the next generation?”
The community became silent. His questions touched the hearts of both young and old.
He continued:
“We may come from different families and communities, but we share one home and one future. If we choose peace today, our children will inherit hope tomorrow.”
The elders, women, youth, and community leaders began talking to one another. They listened to each other's pain, admitted their mistakes, forgave one another, and decided that their differences would no longer be stronger than their humanity.
✓ They began working together, They educated their children, They supported young leaders, They promoted justice and human dignity, They helped one another during difficult times, They worked together in agriculture and small businesses and 
Most importantly, they taught their children that peace is not weakness. it is courage, wisdom, and responsibility.
Slowly, the village began to change.
✓ Where there had once been hatred, there was love, Where there had been division, there was unity, Where there had been discrimination, there was respect, Where there had been injustice, there was a pursuit of social justice, Where there had been hopelessness, there were opportunities and where there had been conflict, there was peace.
The village eventually became an example to surrounding communities. People discovered that development was not impossible; they had simply needed to choose cooperation over division and hope over hatred.
 The Lesson for PANDA!!! 
This story reminds us of what the Peace Action Network for Development Agency (PANDA) stands for: peace, unity, human dignity, justice, education, cooperation, and sustainable development.
As PANDA members, we must never wait for someone else to build the peaceful society we dream of. The change begins with us. Let us educate to understand, lead with integrity, respect one another, forgive, cooperate, and become ambassadors of peace wherever we go.
Moral of the Story
"Peace begins with a choice,  When we choose love over hatred, unity over division, forgiveness over revenge, and cooperation over conflict, we create a future where our communities can prosper."

By Activist Marial Ajiok Athiim!
Juba, South Sudan.
It is deeply disheartening to see a son of the land (Menh Baai) consistently weaponize negative propaganda against his own community elders who occupy vital public offices. Now, more than ever, we need to grant General Akech Tong Aleu the peace of mind required to execute his national duties, rather than systematically trying to pull him down through orchestrated political theater.
After spending the last few hours offline to rest and recover from severe physical exhaustion, I logged onto Facebook only to discover that a known, long-term adversary of Gen. Akech Tong Aleu—someone from Tonj (Menh Tonj)—has once again chosen to mix water with oil, intentionally muddying the political waters.
To be absolutely clear: His Excellency, Governor Gen. Amb. Bol Wek Agoth, is fully occupied with pressing state affairs here in Juba. He has been closely involved in high-level party conferences alongside the other ten state governors and the three chief administrators of the administrative areas. Governor Bol Wek Agoth has absolutely no reason or plans to meet with Akech Tong Aleu regarding the former spy chief currently under house confinement. As the Governor of Warrap State, Amb. Bol’s unyielding priority is to bring an end to the senseless, innocent killings across the three counties of Greater Tonj, ensuring sustainable peace reigns supreme.
Governor Bol Wek Agoth has no hidden political engagements with top leaders in Juba. Every single morning, he joins his fellow governors at the presidency to dedicate his energy to a singular, vital discussion: how lasting peace can prevail across the entire Republic of South Sudan, including Warrap State.
Therefore, I categorically dismiss these toxic allegations as pure fabrications designed to malign two of our top leaders: Gen. Akech Tong Aleu and H.E. Gen. Amb. Bol Wek Agoth.
Notwithstanding these facts, if it is ever discovered that the violence in Tonj is being engineered by senior leaders for personal gain, heavy questions must be answered because this has directly impacted human lives. What remains critical for all of us right now is to bring total peace to Tonj. We must completely abandon these baseless fights that offer no value to our current situation.

To Government officials holding public positions,  
With a direct call to our beloved President Gen. Salva Kiir Mayardit and to My sister Adut Salva Kiir,
BY AKOL MUOR AKOL WITH DISABILITY 
ON 9th July. 2026:
Tel. 0926668750
I stand to speak not only for myself, but for all of us, citizens with disabilities of South Sudan. We are students, teachers, lawyers, nurses, engineers, entrepreneurs, and parents. We are taxpayers, voters, and builders of this nation. Yet when public positions are filled, when boards and commissions are appointed, when ministries make decisions about our lives, we are not in the room. This is not because we lack the qualifications or the will to serve. It is because we are judged by our physical appearance first, and by our capacity last. That judgment is unfair, and it is robbing our country of leaders who are ready to work.
Mr. President, and to all officials currently serving, let us be direct. A wheelchair does not mean a person cannot manage a ministry. A white cane does not mean a person cannot analyze a budget. Deafness does not mean a person has nothing to contribute to policy. Disability is not inability. I am studying Public Administration because I believe I can help run this government better. Many of us have already managed community projects, NGOs, schools, and cooperatives with little support and delivered results. We have solved problems every day simply by navigating a world that was not built for us. That is the kind of resilience, creativity, and accountability that public service requires. Denying us positions because of how we look is denying South Sudan the very skills it needs.
The impact of this exclusion is everywhere. Our right to justice is denied when cases involving persons with disabilities are dismissed as too difficult. Our concerns as citizens are rejected when we ask for accessible offices, transport, and information and are told there is no budget. Health centers are built without ramps. Schools open without inclusive learning materials. Recruitment calls go out with no mention of reasonable accommodation. This happens because the people who live these barriers are not part of the decisions. When you govern without us, you govern blindly. And when you govern blindly, you fail the very people you are sworn to serve.
To you, the government officials holding public positions today, I ask for change that can be seen. Open your ministries to qualified persons with disabilities. Include us in shortlists for director, commissioner, advisor, and management roles. Make government buildings accessible so that once we are appointed, we can actually do the work. Enforce inclusive hiring in every state and national institution. Judge us by our degrees, our experience, our integrity, and our commitment to this country, not by how we enter a room. Leadership is not about appearance. It is about service.
This is why I, Akol Muor Akol, am making a direct appeal to our beloved President Gen. Salva Kiir Mayardit and to Mama Adut Salva Kiir. Mr. President, you have led this nation through war and through peace, and you understand what it means to fight for inclusion. We are asking you now to fight for us. Please issue a presidential directive that mandates the appointment of qualified persons with disabilities to national and state positions. Instruct all ministries to report on inclusive recruitment. Mama Adut, you have always been a voice for the dignity of families and the vulnerable. We ask you to intervene with us, to speak for us, and to ensure that persons with disabilities are given the rights and consideration we deserve as citizens.
We are not asking for pity. We are demanding fairness. We are not asking for special treatment. We are demanding equal opportunity. I am a student today, but I am also a future public servant. Give us the chance to serve now. Put persons with disabilities in government positions, and watch what we can do for South Sudan. Mr. President, Mama Adut, and to every official listening, include us. A nation is only as strong as its commitment to all its people, and we are ready to do our part.
Concern citizen with disability
